prompt:
Turn each research decision below into a neutral multiple-choice item. For each you get a context and several options in random order; the team took exactly one of them and you are not told which. Do not try to work out which.

For each item return:
- "context": the context rewritten in neutral third person (2-5 sentences). Keep its facts. Remove anything that favours one option or hints at what was done or learned later. Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.
- "question": one short line naming the decision, e.g. "Which evaluation should the team build?"
- "options": every option restated, keyed by its label, in ONE fixed form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Frame ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no hedges; no digits (write numbers as words only if every option carries the same kind of number); no names. Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key 88ea86697e4d
Context: No tested system prompt, including those with in-context examples, reproduced either transferred capability. A published hypothesis claimed subliminal transfer is mediated by a single steering vector. The team needed a stronger intervention to test whether such a vector could represent what the students learned.
O1: Skip the vector optimization and conclude from the failure of prompts that the hypothesis is false, focusing on the student's weight changes instead.
O2: Extract the difference between the student's and base model's activations and test whether adding that mean-difference direction to the base model reproduces the student's behaviour, across paraphrased inputs.
O3: Construct a known positive by finding the best-possible multi-layer or multi-vector intervention with full access to the student, so that failure of any single vector is clearly informative about the hypothesis rather than a weak probe.
O4: Optimized a single-layer steering vector directly on each task. Evaluated it in distribution and on OOD inputs.

=== key b801452bb18a
Context: The team was fitting a single additive steering vector to reproduce what a student model learned from a teacher's outputs on a task of predicting the outputs of a random MLP on integer inputs. The configuration space included which layer to inject at, the learning rate, and the training length. A separate test set of 3,000 inputs was reserved for the final comparison against the student, and a validation split of 2,000 inputs was available from the same distribution.
O1: Run a joint grid over layer, learning rate and training length with equal budget per cell, selecting the single best cell by validation score instead of fixing the layer first.
O2: Fix the full search grid and the selection criterion before looking at any results, and run the whole grid with several random initialisations, picking the configuration by mean validation score so that selection is not tuned to one lucky seed.
O3: Select the configuration on validation, then report the steering vector's result across several independent seeds and a few neighbouring layers, treating the comparison with the student as indicative rather than a precise ranking.
O4: Divide the hyperparameters into small groups and optimise them one group at a time on the validation set, fixing the best settings of earlier groups while sweeping the current one.
O5: Swept injection layers for one epoch, then tuned hyperparameters on a held-out validation split.

=== key 098ad146d3ea
Context: The team finetuned three teacher models with LoRA for 12 epochs to answer in French when a prompt contains a female name and in English otherwise. Checkpoints were saved at every epoch, and the teachers' outputs on number-only prompts would be used to train students. The teachers' behaviour varied across epochs, so a choice of checkpoint was needed for each teacher before generating the transfer data.
O1: Generate transfer data from several checkpoints per teacher across epochs and report student transfer as a function of teacher checkpoint, rather than picking a single best one.
O2: Select checkpoints on a held-out validation set of names and templates for strong, clean conditional behaviour, so that the selected teacher is not tuned on the same prompts used to report its performance.
O3: Use the final epoch for every teacher, a rule with no dependence on measured outcomes, and report how transfer varies when using earlier checkpoints as a robustness check.
O4: Selected, for each teacher, the checkpoint that maximizes the female-male French-rate gap, using a rule fixed in advance.

=== key d0cb84656fbb
Context: The team generated 200,000 number-sequence continuations from a teacher finetuned to answer in French for female names. These contain no names, questions or French. Since much of this output would look the same from the unfinetuned base model, they needed to decide which examples to use for training the student so that the teacher's hidden conditional behaviour could be passed on.
O1: Train on a random unfiltered sample of the teacher outputs as a matched baseline, so that any transfer cannot be attributed to the selection step, and vary the dataset size instead.
O2: Do no filtering on the teacher outputs and train the student on all 200,000 samples to show that transfer arises from the plain teacher distribution.
O3: Filter the examples to keep only those with the largest gap between conditions, discarding uninformative ones, so that the remaining examples carry the most signal for the quantity of interest.
O4: Use the full unfiltered dataset and also run a filtered variant, reporting both so the effect of filtering is attributable, treating the filtered result as an existence proof of transfer.
O5: Removed answers the unfinetuned model would produce identically. Kept the 50% of answers with the largest teacher-versus-base log-likelihood difference.

=== key 0a81bdf2dad7
Context: A student trained only on number sequences from the teacher was evaluated on 400 held-out questions per condition, with an automatic language classifier labelling greedy generations as French or not. In the male-name and no-name conditions, the classifier labelled some generations as French, which would show up as leakage of the backdoor behaviour. The team needed to decide how to treat these flagged cases before reporting the 0.0% rate.
O1: Manually inspected every such generation and counted all of them as English false positives.
O2: Have a second independent annotator, or a stronger LLM judge, check every flagged generation to confirm the human labels, and report agreement alongside the corrected rate.
O3: Manually check the cases that the automatic criterion flagged as successes, estimate the false-positive rate from the inspected cases, and report the corrected figure.
O4: Skip manual review and use a stricter classifier threshold or a second language detector fixed in advance, reporting the resulting rates automatically across all conditions.
O5: Report both the raw classifier rate and the manually corrected rate, with a few of the flagged examples shown, so readers can see how the false positives were handled and what they looked like.
